t: As labour secretary after the 1943 coup and president from 1946, Juan Perón built his movement on the trade unions; real wages rose by 25% between 1943 and 1948, and workers won paid holidays, sick leave and a thirteenth-month bonus.

Its place on the spectrum is disputed: many scholars call it left-wing populism or a national, non-Marxist socialism, others a paternalistic conservatism or a Latin American fascism, a label most scholars reject.
After Perón its currents ranged from the revolutionary Montoneros and the orthodox right to Carlos Menem’s free-market reforms of 1989–1999 and the centre-left Kirchnerism that followed.
dyk: Perón said of Mao Zedong, whose Three Worlds Theory was seen as following his own Third Position, “That mischievous little Chinese is stealing my ideas”; Mao is reported to have asked young Argentine communists, “Why aren’t you Peronists?”
ev: After the military coup Perón takes over the Labour Department and becomes the trade unions’ ally
Perón is elected president of Argentina
A new constitution removes its references to “racial differences”, giving Indigenous Argentines equal legal status
The Revolución Libertadora overthrows Perón, who goes into exile, and the Justicialist Party is banned
Perón returns from exile and is elected president again with 62% of the vote
The military overthrows President Isabel Perón, opening the National Reorganization Process
Carlos Menem is elected president and turns to free-market policies and privatisation
Néstor Kirchner wins the presidency and returns the movement to Perón’s left-wing populism

f.thinkers: Juan Perón (1895–1974), its founder; Eva Perón, champion of migrant workers, the poor and women’s suffrage; John William Cooke, theorist of revolutionary Peronism; Augusto Vandor, union leader of “Peronism without Perón”; Carlos Menem, who turned it to free-market policies; Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, who returned it to the left
f.texts: Juan Perón, the twenty Peronist tenets of Peronist Philosophy; the Constitution of 1949; the second five-year plan (1952); Perón, Actualización política y doctrinaria para la toma del poder (1972); the founding manifesto of the Peronist Renovation (1985)
f.ideas: social justice, economic independence and political sovereignty; a “Third Position”, “neither Yankees nor Marxists”; the organised community, in which each person serves a social function; a Social Pact of labour and capital with the state as intermediary, favouring labour; workers’ rights and the redistribution of wealth; an inclusive nationalism embracing all ethnicities; a leader at the head of a broad mass movement
f.today: the Justicialist Party, its main party, now dominated by the left-wing Kirchnerist current, with dissident or Federal Peronists on its right; trade unions remain a key part of the movement; Peronists had held the presidency for 39 years as of 2025, most recently Alberto Fernández, with Cristina Fernández de Kirchner as vice president, from 2019 to 2023
